title: British lichen records shifted to warmer niches in 1965-2025 through fewer cool-niche species, not more warm-niche species; a larger shift at high 1970 SO2 was absent in bark-focused visits
abstract: We tested whether the rise of warm-niche lichens in north-western European records follows climate warming or the recovery after sulphur dioxide (SO2) decrease. We rebuilt the species lists of 184,112 British Lichen Society visits (GBIF) from facet counts and gave 1,268 species a temperature index (STI) from their European GBIF range and CRU climate. With 0.1-degree cell fixed effects and list-length terms, the community temperature index (CTI) of 57,022 visits rose by about 0.12-0.17 C from 1965-1984 to 2010-2025, which is about 15-45% of full tracking of the 1.04 C warming. The rise came from fewer cool-niche species (STI below 7 C), not from more warm-niche species: the warm-niche share changed by 0 to +1.8 percentage points, and van Herk's warm indicators did not increase as a group. In pooled visits the rise was larger at high 1970 SO2 emission density (0.25 C, SE 0.045, against 0.065 C, SE 0.028), and species trends rose with STI only in formerly polluted cells (+0.11 log-odds per C). But this SO2 gradient was absent in bark-focused visits (-0.034 C per SD, SE 0.032) and in England, it reversed in 1998-2009, and it did not occur with the CBED sulphur-deposition decrease, NHx deposition or local warming. Thus the shift is spatially broad and is not a warm-species spread. Limitations: opportunistic records without substrate, habitat change within cells, shorter lists after 2010, and national drivers that this design cannot separate from recording change.

Same 0.1-degree cells, list-length adjusted; bands are 95% CI. In bark-focused visits the CTI rose by a similar amount in clean and polluted cells.

Change from 1965-1984 to 2010-2025 at low (10th percentile) and high (90th percentile) exposure for CTI, warm-niche share and cool-niche share, by exposure and visit set. Only the local 1970 SO2 emission proxy gave a larger change at high exposure, and not in bark-focused visits.

Contributions of species, grouped by species temperature index, to the CTI change in visits with 10-30 records. Most of the rise came from fewer species with STI below 7 C; warm-niche gains and losses nearly cancelled.
